::::{.cr-section layout="sidebar-right"}

@cr-rationale

::: {#cr-rationale .large-fixed-text-left}
Understanding the progression of <span style="color:#6EAB8A">*AI*</span> and <span style="color:#6EAB8A">*Machine Learning*</span> development in the Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance field
:::

![](stethoscope.gif){width="100%"}
::::

:::::

::::{.cr-section layout="overlay-center"}

:::{#cr-photo1 .fullpage}
![](cardiac.jpg)
:::

:::{.progress-block}

Artificial Intelligence has transformed medical imaging, and cardiac MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) is one of the most active frontiers. @cr-photo1

It is essential to examine how research on cardiovascular imaging methods development has evolved recently and how knowledge within this field is being generated.

By utilizing text analysis and natural language processing, we can interpret large volumes of textual data regarding design, development, manufacture, and evaluation of cardiovascular imaging technologies. 

Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (JCMR) is a leading publication site for basic and clinical research on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) methods.

Our goal is to transform this large of unstructured data into well‐organized and meaningful insights. We want to highlight the growing role of AI and Machine Learning in the development of CMR, particularly for audiences outside the research and medical imaging communities.

:::
::::

::::{.cr-section layout="sidebar-right"}
@cr-linechart

:::{#cr-linechart}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 6

jcmr_yearly <- jcmr |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date),
         year = lubridate::year(date)) |>
  filter(!is.na(keyword), !is.na(year)) |>
  group_by(year, keyword) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")


lineplot <- ggplot(jcmr_yearly, aes(x = year, y = n, color = keyword)) +
  geom_point(aes(group = seq_along(year)),
             size = 4,
             alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(aes(lty = keyword), linewidth = 1.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "machine learning" = "seagreen",
    "deep learning" = "skyblue",
    "artificial intelligence" = "cornflowerblue",
    "convolution" = "#A67BB8"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth of AI-Related Publications in JCMR",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Articles",
    color = "Keyword"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
  panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  text = element_text(color = "black"),
  legend.position = "bottom",
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

lineplot +
  transition_reveal(along = year) 
```
:::

Before 2012, publications mentioning any of these keywords were pretty rare. Convolution was actually the most common term early on, which makes sense because convolutional methods in image processing predate the modern AI boom by quite a bit.

Around 2012 to 2016, convolution peaks and then starts to drop off. This is right around the time deep learning started taking over as the dominant approach, so researchers were moving away from older convolutional methods and toward neural network based ones.

The really dramatic shift happens right after 2020. Machine learning shoots up faster than any other keyword, hitting over 10 articles in a single year. This is when COVID pushed a lot of medical research toward automation and AI.

What is also interesting is that artificial intelligence and deep learning both start climbing steeply around the same time, but machine learning stays ahead. So even as the field got more sophisticated, researchers still preferred the broader term machine learning when describing their work rather than getting more specific.

By 2023 all four keywords are appearing at much higher rates than they were even five years earlier showing how fast the field is moving.

@cr-barchart-unigram

:::{#cr-barchart-unigram}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 8

# Stop words setup
cmr_stopword <- c("study", "scientific", "high", "increased", "induced", 
                  "levels", "expression", "potential", "treatment", "related", 
                  "significantly", "accumulation", "showed", "specific", "yrs", 
                  "age", "effect", "effects", "results", "analysis", "revealed", 
                  "human", "1", "2", "3", "group", "formation", "reduced", 
                  "function", "decreased", "model", "fat", "compared", "based", 
                  "size", "stability", "assessment", "method", "clinical", 
                  "activity", "findings", "mechanisms", "energy", "exposure", 
                  "content", "properties", "development", "higher", "metabolic", 
                  "disease", "recovery", "cellular", "significant", "including", 
                  "dependent", "independent", "patients", "background", 
                  "objectives", "recent", "studies", "information")

full_stopwords <- data.frame(
  word = cmr_stopword,
  lexicon = rep("custom", times = length(cmr_stopword))
)

stop_words_fix <- dplyr::bind_rows(stop_words, full_stopwords)

remove_word <- c("cmr", "cardiovascular", "data", "contrast", "images", 
                 "image", "imaging", "blood", "learning", "magnetic", 
                 "resonance", "flow", "approach", "accuracy")

jcmr |>
  filter(!is.na(abstract)) |>
  select(keyword, abstract) |>
  mutate(abstract = str_to_lower(abstract)) |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = abstract) |>
  anti_join(stop_words_fix, by = "word") |>
  filter(!word %in% remove_word) |>
  filter(word != "NA") |>
  count(keyword, word, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(keyword) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 10) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder_within(word, n, keyword), y = n, fill = keyword)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~keyword, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "machine learning"       = "seagreen",
    "deep learning"          = "skyblue",
    "artificial intelligence" = "cornflowerblue",
    "convolution"            = "#A67BB8"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Frequent Words in Abstracts by Keyword",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
:::

Across all keywords, words like "myocardial," "perfusion," and "quantification" appear frequently, which shows us the main focus of cardiac MRI research.

In "machine learning" abstracts, "myocardial" dominates by a wide margin. 

"Deep learning" abstracts highlight "coronary" and "strain" quite prominently, which points to a focus on coronary artery imaging and cardiac motion analysis.

"Artificial intelligence" abstracts focus on "lv" (left ventricle) and "ventricular" function, so AI is might be most often applied to measuring heart chamber performance.

"Convolution" abstracts stand out with focusing mainly on "perfusion" and "3d" which appear frequently, indicating a focus on blood flow imaging.

@cr-barchart-allgram

:::{#cr-barchart-allgram}

```{r}
# Stop words setup
cmr_stopword <- c("study", "scientific", "high", "increased", "induced", 
                  "levels", "expression", "potential", "treatment", "related", 
                  "significantly", "accumulation", "showed", "specific", "yrs", 
                  "age", "effect", "effects", "results", "analysis", "revealed", 
                  "human", "1", "2", "3", "group", "formation", "reduced", 
                  "function", "decreased", "model", "fat", "compared", "based", 
                  "size", "stability", "assessment", "method", "clinical", 
                  "activity", "findings", "mechanisms", "energy", "exposure", 
                  "content", "properties", "development", "higher", "metabolic", 
                  "disease", "recovery", "cellular", "significant", "including", 
                  "dependent", "independent", "patients", "background", 
                  "objectives", "recent", "studies", "information")

full_stopwords <- data.frame(
  word = cmr_stopword,
  lexicon = rep("custom", times = length(cmr_stopword))
)

stop_words_fix <- dplyr::bind_rows(stop_words, full_stopwords)

remove_word <- c("cmr", "cardiovascular", "data", "contrast", "images", 
                 "image", "imaging", "blood", "learning", "magnetic", 
                 "resonance", "flow", "approach", "accuracy")

remove_bigram_words <- c("cmr", "cardiovascular", "magnetic", "resonance", 
                          "imaging", "images", "mri", "image", "cardiac",
                          "learning", "flow", "lge", "dl", "jcmr", 
                          "articles", "pool", "stimulated", "echoes",
                          "rtof", "pc", "af")

# Build clean bigrams
abstract_bigram_clean <- jcmr |>
  filter(!is.na(abstract)) |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, abstract, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!str_detect(bigram, "^\\d")) |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE) |>
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") |>
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words_fix$word,
         !word2 %in% stop_words_fix$word) |>
  filter(!word1 %in% remove_bigram_words,
         !word2 %in% remove_bigram_words) |>
  filter(!is.na(word1) & !is.na(word2)) |>
  filter(n >= 3)

# Bigram descriptions
bigram_descriptions <- tribble(
  ~bigram,                  ~description,
  "blood flow",             "Movement of blood through cardiac vessels",
  "deep learning",          "AI method using layered neural networks",
  "myocardial perfusion",   "Blood flow through heart muscle tissue",
  "myocardial blood",       "Blood supply to the heart muscle",
  "coronary artery",        "Main blood vessels supplying the heart",
  "time consuming",         "Refers to slow traditional analysis methods AI aims to replace",
  "left ventricular",       "Relating to the heart's main pumping chamber",
  "t1 mapping",             "MRI technique measuring tissue water content",
  "free breathing",         "MRI acquired without requiring breath holds",
  "breath hold",            "Technique to reduce motion blur in MRI scans",
  "artificial intelligence","Computer systems performing human-like analysis tasks",
  "phase contrast",         "MRI technique for measuring blood flow velocity",
  "myocardial t1",          "T1 relaxation time measured in heart muscle",
  "myocardial fibrosis",    "Scarring of heart muscle tissue",
  "machine learning",       "AI method that learns patterns from data",
  "left atrial",            "Relating to the upper left chamber of the heart",
  "filling curves",         "Measures how the heart fills with blood",
  "ejection fraction",      "Percentage of blood pumped out per heartbeat",
  "arterial input",         "Blood supply entering a region of tissue",
  "atrial fibrillation",    "Irregular heartbeat affecting the upper chambers"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

bigram_plot <- abstract_bigram_clean |>
  unite(bigram, word1, word2, sep = " ") |>
  slice_max(n, n = 20) |>
  left_join(bigram_descriptions, by = "bigram") |>
  mutate(
    description = ifelse(is.na(description), "No description available", description),
    hover_text = paste0("<b>", bigram, "</b><br>Count: ", n, "<br><i>", description, "</i>")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(bigram, n), y = n, fill = bigram, text = hover_text)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Frequent Two Word Combinations in Abstracts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggplotly(bigram_plot, tooltip = "text")
```
:::

"Blood flow" and "deep learning" are the two most common bigrams by a pretty wide margin. This makes a lot of sense when you think about it beacuse the whole point of most of this research is figuring out how to use AI to understand how blood moves through the heart more efficiently than before.

What is interesting is that "time consuming" shows up this high on the list. Researchers keep bringing it up because traditional cardiac MRI analysis required specialists to sit down and manually trace heart structures for hours. A huge part of why AI became so appealing in this field is simply that it promised to make that process way faster and less dependent on one person doing it correctly.

Word pairs like "myocardial perfusion" and "coronary artery" are the core vocabulary of cardiac MRI research. These are the specific measurements doctors need to make when figuring out whether a heart is functioning properly or showing signs of disease.

Hover over any bar to see what that word combination actually means.

```{r}
abstract_trigram_clean <- jcmr |>

trigram_descriptions <- tribble(
```

::::{.cr-section layout="sidebar-right"}
@cr-barchart-trigram

:::{#cr-barchart-trigram}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

trigram_plot <- abstract_trigram_clean |>
  slice_max(n, n = 20) |>
  left_join(trigram_descriptions, by = "trigram") |>
  mutate(
    description = ifelse(is.na(description), "No description available", description),
    hover_text = paste0("<b>", trigram, "</b><br>Count: ", n, "<br><i>", description, "</i>")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(trigram, n), y = n, fill = trigram, text = hover_text)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Frequent Three Word Combinations in Abstracts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

ggplotly(trigram_plot, tooltip = "text")
```

:::

"Myocardial blood flow" is so far ahead of everything else on this chart that it basically summarizes what most of this research is about. At the end of the day, the most important question in cardiology is whether enough blood is reaching the heart muscle, and a huge portion of the AI research in JCMR is trying to measure that more accurately and automatically.

"Late gadolinium enhancement" in second makes a lot of sense too. It is one of the oldest and most established MRI techniques for detecting scarring and damage in the heart, so it comes up constantly as a reference point that newer AI methods are trying to match or improve on.

One of the more interesting phrases lower down the list is "inter observer variability." This refers to the problem of two doctors looking at the exact same scan and coming up with different measurements. It is a well known issue in radiology and it is exactly the kind of inconsistency that AI is well suited to reduce, since a model will always give the same answer for the same input.

Hover over any bar to see a plain English explanation of what each three word phrase means in the context of cardiac MRI research.

@cr-network

:::{#cr-network}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 8

remove_bigram_words <- c("cmr", "cardiovascular", "magnetic", "resonance", "imaging", "images", "mri", "image", "cardiac", "learning", "flow", "lge", "dl", "jcmr", "articles", "pool", "stimulated", "echoes", "rtof", "pc", "af")

abstract_bigram_clean <- jcmr |>
  filter(!is.na(abstract)) |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, abstract, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  filter(!str_detect(bigram, "^\\d")) |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE) |>
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") |>
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words_fix$word,
         !word2 %in% stop_words_fix$word) |>
  filter(!word1 %in% remove_bigram_words,
         !word2 %in% remove_bigram_words) |>
  filter(!is.na(word1) & !is.na(word2)) |>
  filter(n >= 3)

bigram_graph <- abstract_bigram_clean |>
  graph_from_data_frame()

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n), show.legend = FALSE, color = "seagreen", arrow = arrow(length = unit(3, "mm"))) +
  geom_node_point(color = "cornflowerblue", size = 4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3.5, color = "black") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Network of Most Common Word Pairs in Abstracts")
```
:::

Each line between two words means they appeared next to each other frequently in the abstracts, so the stronger the connection, the more often that pair showed up together.

The biggest cluster on the right tells us that "myocardial" connects to "perfusion," "fibrosis," "blood," and "t1". These are main things researchers are trying 
to measure in the heart muscle using AI.

On the bottom left, "ventricular" branches out to "lv," "rv," "left," and "filling" which are all different ways of describing and measuring the heart's chambers.

"Coronary" links to "artery" and "angiography," so imaging the coronary arteries is potentially its own distinct research thread separate from the heart muscle work happening on the other side of the graph.

Isolated pairs like "gadolinium enhancement" and "ejection fraction" are well-known clinical terms that always appear together.

::::{.cr-section layout="sidebar-right"}
@cr-treemap

:::{#cr-treemap}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(plotly)


treemap_data <- jcmr |>
  filter(!is.na(abstract)) |>
  mutate(abstract = str_to_lower(abstract)) |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = abstract) |>
  anti_join(stop_words_fix, by = "word") |>
  filter(!word %in% remove_word) |>
  filter(!word %in% remove_bigram_words) |>
  filter(word != "NA") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 30)

plot_ly(
  data = treemap_data,
  type = "treemap",
  labels = ~word,
  values = ~n,
  parents = ""
)
```
:::

When you look across all of the abstracts together, "myocardial," "heart," and "perfusion" take up the most space. This makes sense because most of this research comes down to one question if the heart is receiving enough blood. 

"Segmentation," "strain," and "mapping" are some of the more interesting mid-sized boxes because these are the specific tasks AI is actually being used to automate. Segmentation means tracing the outline of the heart in an image, strain means measuring how much the heart wall moves, and mapping means creating a picture of tissue properties across the whole heart.

"3d," "4d," and "automated" showing up this prominently tells you about where the field is headed, since more research is aimed to happen automatically in three and four dimensions, which is a complex process in which AI is being included.
